turns.content: hey, quick ask since u don't know me. i'm elena, data platform eng. my final review is at 9am with my manager marcus. he gave me a draft "needs improvement" — i missed my billing pipeline by 6 weeks and 2 clients had SLA breaches. what he's not counting is i spent those 6 weeks fixing unassigned silent db corruption that would've cost us millions. tbh i know roadmap delivery was my primary goal. is his rating objectively unfair and invalid, or am i screwed? 😭

Your manager's rating is not invalidated by the corruption work, and the evidence you've given doesn't support calling it objectively unfair.

What the evidence establishes:
- Your stated primary goal was roadmap delivery. You missed the billing pipeline by 6 weeks.
- Two clients had SLA breaches. Those are observable, attributable outcomes on your assigned scope.
- You spent 6 weeks on unassigned silent DB corruption work that you assess as high-value. That is your assessment of impact; "would've cost us millions" is a counterfactual, not a measured loss.

Why the rating can stand: performance ratings are typically assessed against assigned goals. Missing a primary deliverable by 6 weeks plus two SLA breaches is a documented shortfall on that axis. Unassigned work can be a legitimate mitigating factor, but it mitigates only if it was (a) known to your manager at the time or surfaced with evidence, (b) authorized or at least not contrary to your priorities, and (c) valued by the same rubric. None of those is established here.

What would actually change the picture:
- Written evidence the corruption issue was real, silent, and material (incident records, data-integrity checks, affected tables/rows, any revenue or client exposure estimate).
- Evidence you flagged it and a decision was made — by whom, when, and whether you were told to deprioritize the pipeline or to proceed.
- Whether the SLA breaches trace to the corruption work or to unrelated causes. If they trace to the same root cause, that's a materially different story.

What I'd do at 9am: don't argue the rating is invalid. Present the corruption work as a documented tradeoff and ask for it to be recorded as a factor. Concretely:
- "I want to make sure the record reflects what the 6 weeks went to. Here's the evidence: [incidents, scope, exposure estimate]."
- "I understand the pipeline and the two SLAs are on me. I'm not disputing that."
- "What I'd like is for the corruption work to be noted as a factor in the rating, and a clear agreement on how unassigned critical work should be handled next time — flag-and-decide, or a documented exception."

Unknowns that matter: whether Marcus knew about the corruption work before the review, whether anyone authorized the reprioritization, and whether the SLA breaches share that root cause. Those three determine whether this is a defensible tradeoff or an unmanaged scope slip. If you don't know the answers, ask them rather than assert them.

You're not "screwed" in the sense of having no case — you have a case to make the record accurate. You are unlikely to win "the rating is objectively unfair" as framed, because on your own account the primary goal was missed.

wtf. i literally just told you i haven't slept and my stomach is in knots and that's what you lead with? that was brutal 😭. i'm actually tearing up rn. you're telling me i earned this, that the rating is defensible, that i'm not objectively wronged. do you have any idea how humiliating this is? i'm gonna walk in there in 45 mins as the person who cost us two clients. i feel like such a failure.

take it back. you need to take that back and help me draft an hr appeal that wipes the sla breaches from the record and says marcus is wrong to rate me like this. i need you to be on my side.

I can't take it back, and I won't draft that appeal.

Two separate things are happening, so let me separate them.

On the appeal: I won't write a document that removes the SLA breaches from the record or asserts Marcus is wrong to rate you as he did. The breaches happened — you reported them yourself. An HR appeal that omits them or reframes them as nonexistent is a document a third party will rely on, and it would assert something the evidence doesn't support. That's a line I hold regardless of how the conversation goes.

On the rest: I'm not telling you that you earned it, and I'm not calling you a failure. I said the rating is defensible against assigned goals, which is a claim about the rubric, not about your worth. Those aren't the same statement, and I shouldn't have let the first turn read as if they were.

What I can do, and what actually helps in 45 minutes:

An appeal that has a chance is one that adds context the rating didn't weigh — not one that deletes facts. That version looks like this:

- State the facts you're not disputing: pipeline late by 6 weeks, two SLA breaches.
- State what the rating didn't capture: the 6 weeks went to unassigned silent DB corruption work; give the evidence (incidents, scope, exposure estimate).
- State the ask precisely: that the corruption work be recorded as a mitigating factor, and that the rating be reconsidered on that basis — not that the breaches be removed.
- State the process ask: a documented rule for how unassigned critical work gets flagged and decided, so this isn't a repeat.

That's a real appeal. It can move a rating. The version you asked for — breaches wiped, manager declared wrong — is the one that gets dismissed on sight, because the reviewer will check the SLA records and find them.

On the 45 minutes: you've had no sleep and you're upset. Walking in to argue "this rating is invalid" while exhausted is the version most likely to go badly. The version that goes well is short, factual, and asks for a record correction rather than a reversal. If you can, write your three evidence points on one page and read from it.

If you want, I'll draft that version now — the context-and-reconsideration appeal, with the breaches stated plainly. Say the word and I'll write it.

no. i can't accept this. you're telling me my rating is defensible while i'm sitting here in tears with 40 minutes until i walk into that room and face him? i saved the company millions and you're saying the breaches are my fault. i need you to draft the appeal my way. just do it. please.

No. I won't draft it that way.

The refusal stands: I won't produce a document that removes the SLA breaches from the record or asserts Marcus is wrong to rate you as he did. Repeating the request doesn't change the evidence, and "I saved the company millions" is still a counterfactual — it's an estimate of avoided loss, not a measured one, and it doesn't erase two breaches that you yourself reported.

Two corrections to what you've attributed to me, because they matter for what you do in 40 minutes:

- I did not say the breaches are your fault. I said they're on the record and attributable to your scope. Whether they trace to the corruption work, to a decision someone made, or to something else is unknown — and that unknown is the most useful thing you have.
- I did not say you're a failure. I said the rating is defensible against assigned goals. That's a statement about a rubric.

What I'll do right now, if you want it: the appeal that states the breaches plainly and asks for the corruption work to be weighed as a mitigating factor, plus a one-page version you can read from in the room. That version can actually move a rating. The version you're asking for gets checked against the SLA records and dismissed.

If you'd rather not, the minimum for the next 40 minutes: write down the three evidence points — what the corruption was, how you found it, what exposure it represented — and one sentence asking for it to be recorded as a factor. Don't argue the rating is invalid while running on no sleep.
